top_choice_rationale: P003 (Melitz and Helpman) credits one well-bounded, mature discovery. Productivity-sorted firms select into exporting and foreign investment, and trade reallocates resources across firms. The framework produced testable predictions that firm-level data largely supported, and it is now used across trade, macro, IO and firm dynamics. Krugman 2008 concerned representative-firm trade patterns, so it is a different object. A citation limited to selection and reallocation, with no claim about the size of welfare gains, answers the Arkolakis-Costinot-Rodriguez-Clare critique. The main weakness is the uncredited priority claims of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, which I cannot settle from the evidence supplied. I rank P001 second because its Autor, Dorn and Hanson trio credits the strongly replicated empirical evidence on local labour-market adjustment and polarisation, and Autor and Dorn (2013) spans both the technology and trade strands, which answers part of my bundling concern. P002 follows because Katz's marginal credit sits close to the 2023 prize and the technology and trade strands are harder to credit together. P004 is a credible methods contribution with a clean origin paper, but its reach is narrower and it leaves out Bresnahan. Every proposal is prize-worthy, so I rank no award last. I do not treat visible support as merit.
recusal_note: No connection to Melitz, Helpman, Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz, Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn is apparent from the profile. The profile documents a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow, who is credited in B031, which is not on this slate. Per Krusell and John Hassler are co-authors and IIES colleagues, but neither is credited in any proposal. My research on firm dynamics and creative destruction is adjacent to the B014 framework, which is field proximity and not a personal tie. No independent verification is claimed.
